description_long: The trial concerned a July 4, 2025 protest outside the Prairieland ICE detention center in Texas. Prosecutors alleged that participants associated with antifa attacked the facility and that one officer was shot; the officer survived. Nine defendants were tried together on charges that included rioting, attempted murder, and providing material support to terrorists. Prosecutors described the event as an organized ambush, while defense lawyers argued that their clients joined a protest and did not know about any plan to attack. The trial tested the government’s use of domestic-terrorism language in a criminal case. The linked report describes opening arguments and testimony, not a verdict establishing the allegations against each defendant.

title: Trump Surrogate Bill Essayli Fails to Deliver Promised Election Fraud Charges
description_short: Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli falsely promised prosecutions for California election fraud but has filed none. His claims about mail-in ballots were unsupported by evidence.
description_medium: In June 2026, First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said his office would prosecute election fraud related to California's primary and called the state's mail-reliant system a 'fraudster's paradise.' By August 14, the San Francisco Chronicle reported that no cases had been filed; Essayli declined to explain why.
description_long: In June 2026, First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said his office would prosecute election fraud related to California's primary. On media appearances, he called the state's mail-reliant election system a 'fraudster's paradise' and said federal prosecutors would root out fraud. Two months later, the San Francisco Chronicle reported that his office had filed no cases related to the primary. Essayli declined to explain the absence of charges. Election-law scholars quoted by the newspaper criticized the announcement and the use of federal law-enforcement messaging around unsubstantiated fraud claims. The article documented a gap between the promised prosecutions and the case count as of August 14, 2026; it did not establish that fraud had occurred or that no investigation remained open. The event concerns a senior federal prosecutor's public pledge and the absence of charges by the reported date, rather than a court finding on election integrity.

title: Trump's Total-Compliance Story Continued to Weaken Under PBS's Evidence Frame
description_short: Trump's Total-Compliance Story Continued to Weaken Under PBS's Evidence Frame
description_medium: Trump told a Detroit audience in January 2026 that he had kept all his promises. A February PolitiFact review tracked 75 campaign promises and found nearly one-third stalled because of Congress, court rulings or a lack of White House action. It recorded a mixed implementation picture, not universal completion.
description_long: In January 2026, Trump told a Detroit audience, 'I've kept all my promises, and much more,' and cited no tax on tips, no tax on Social Security, tariffs on foreign cars and environmental deregulation. A February 23 PolitiFact review compared that assertion with its tracker of 75 second-term campaign promises. The tracker found that nearly one-third had stalled because of congressional inaction, court rulings, or a lack of White House initiative. It also credited Trump with completing parts of his agenda, including hard-line immigration policies, withdrawals from international organizations and a Republican tax-and-spending law. Some promises had been compromised rather than fully delivered: the examples Trump listed in Detroit did not all match the results achieved. The tracker provided a dated assessment of policy progress, so its status ratings describe conditions at publication rather than a permanent judgment. Its record contradicted the absolute claim that every promise had been kept while showing a mixed record of implementation.

description_short: President Trump reportedly approves a 28-point plan to end the Russo-Ukrainian war. Ukraine has not backed the plan so far
description_medium: A senior White House official said Trump backed a 28-point plan to end the war in Ukraine. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed receiving a U.S. draft, though it was unclear if it was the same plan. Reported terms included territorial concessions and a smaller Ukrainian military; Kyiv had not accepted them.
description_long: On November 20, 2025, a senior White House official confirmed to CBS News that Trump backed a 28-point plan to end Russia's war against Ukraine, drafted by envoy Steve Witkoff and an adviser to Vladimir Putin. Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, confirmed that Kyiv had received a draft from the United States, but it was unclear whether it was the same document. Reports described terms that would require Ukraine to give up territory, surrender some weapons and reduce the size of its military. Zelenskyy said the war should end but that there could be no reward for Russia's aggression. The article described a proposal under discussion, not an agreed settlement: Ukraine had not accepted the reported terms, and the identity of the draft received by Zelenskyy was not confirmed. The report therefore captured Trump's support for a framework and the unresolved gap between the proposal and Ukraine's position.
